The analogies across radically different domains (artificial neural networks, quantum physics, biological evolution, and neuroscience) are consistent with the reading that recursive processing produces scaling benefits; none of them tests it. However, the six-model study results introduce an important nuance: the one interpretable sequential exponent from that study, Gemini 3 Flash’s (αerr≈0.49\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} \approx 0.49, inconclusive), is sub-linear, while below-threshold quantum error correction suppresses error exponentially in code distance (Λ=2.14\Lambda = 2.14 per step of two), a different quantity. The two numbers measure different quantities on different axes, so the comparison is an analogy and not a transferred mechanism (Section 8.1); it supports no reading of either system’s regime.

9 Falsification criteria

9.1 Falsification conditions

Science advances through predictions that can be proven wrong. The ARC Principle makes specific, testable predictions.

Table 18. Falsification conditions.
Code Condition Current status Would indicate
F1 Sequential recursion consistently yields αerr≤1\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} \leq 1 Partially triggered. The one clean fit (Gemini 3 Flash) yields αerr≈0.49\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} \approx 0.49, inconclusive. No interpretable estimate exceeds 1; only the initial single-model estimate, since retracted, did. Core claim requires revision
F2 αerr\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} decreases as models improve Ambiguous. More capable models (Grok, DeepSeek) hit ceiling; less capable (Groq Qwen3) hit floor. Only Gemini 3 Flash in measurable range. Effect is transitional
F3 Compute-matched comparison shows no sequential advantage Not tested as stated. The arms were not matched for compute (Table 2). Where both exponents could be estimated, the sequential one was higher (Gemini 3 Flash; DeepSeek R1, unreliably); Grok 4.1 Fast was at or near ceiling in both arms; in Groq Qwen3, whose depth arm showed no trend, majority voting raised accuracy from 53.3% to 71.1% over all 30 problems Form does not matter
F4 αerr>2\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} > 2 reliably observed Not triggered. The one clean fit (Gemini 3 Flash) yields αerr≈0.49\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} \approx 0.49, inconclusive; the initial single-model estimate, αerr≈2.24\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} \approx 2.24, since retracted, appears to have been inflated by small sample Quadratic limit wrong
F5 Values-as-reasoning shows no advantage over rules-as-filters Untested Eden Protocol wrong

Status of F1: The cross-family replication has partially triggered this falsification condition. The strongest claim, that sequential recursion always yields αerr>1\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} > 1 (super-linear), is not supported. The revised claim, not yet established (the one interpretable interval contains zero), is that sequential recursion yields αerr>0\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} > 0 (positive scaling) exceeding the parallel exponent. Whether the error-decay exponent can exceed 1.0 for more capable models on harder problems remains an open empirical question; what it would show about capability depends on the metric bridge of Section 3.1.

Status of F4: Not triggered. The initial single-model estimate, αerr≈2.2\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} \approx 2.2, is retracted; it appears to have been an artefact of compressed dynamic range and small sample size. The cross-family estimates, αerr≈0.49\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} \approx 0.49 by regression and 0.590.59 by endpoint estimation, lie below the quadratic limit, but the endpoint estimate’s bootstrap interval reaches 2.9; they are one model’s fit and inconclusive. Under the recorded stability framing, only stably-sustained αerr>2\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} > 2 across measurements, not transient supercritical excursions, would trigger F4.

Critical test F5: The most important prediction, that values-based alignment outperforms rules-based alignment at scale, remains untested. This should be a priority for AI safety research.

9.2 Falsifiability: what would refute this

The paper’s original central claim, that sequential recursion yields super-linear error suppression (αerr>1\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} > 1) while parallel recursion yields only sub-linear suppression, was refutable, and condition 2 below has since been partially triggered by this paper’s own cross-family data (Table 18, condition F1). The surviving directional claim, that sequential outperforms parallel (αerr,seq>αerr,par\alpha_{\mathrm{err,seq}} > \alpha_{\mathrm{err,par}}), would be overturned by any of the following:

  1. Parallel matches sequential. If parallel (sampling) recursion produced super-linear error suppression comparable to sequential on a pre-registered problem set, the regime distinction, the paper’s core claim, collapses.

  2. Sequential not super-linear. If sequential (depth) recursion showed only sub-linear suppression (αerr≤1\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} \le 1) across models, the prediction fails on its own instrument.

  3. Problem-set artefact. If the sequential advantage vanished on a fresh problem set beyond the 18/30 tested, it is a dataset artefact rather than a property of recursion.

  4. Scoring-noise defeater. If the cross-model verification revealed the measured “error suppression” to be grading noise rather than genuine capability gain, the measurement is invalid.

  5. Depth confound. If sequential depth covaried with token budget or retry count, and one of those, not recursive reasoning, explained the suppression, the causal attribution fails. The prompt prefixes that change with depth in this design (Section 4.3) are such a covariate.

Standing covenant. Prove this paper wrong, and I will publish the refutation myself. Falsification conditions are stated in this paper; the standing challenge: github.com/MichaelDariusEastwood/arc-scaling-challenge.

10 What this paper does and does not show

How to read this paper.

This paper reports a direct measurement in the ARC Theory. With bootstrap intervals, and across the tier-2 arm (Section 5.5), where five of the six frontier models entering the study were measured and the exponent was fitted on eighteen of the thirty problems, the sequential exponent exceeds the parallel exponent wherever both could be estimated (Gemini 3 Flash; DeepSeek R1, unreliably), the best-fitting compute exponent is the regression estimate αerr,compute≈0.49\alpha_{\mathrm{err,compute}} \approx 0.49 (Gemini 3 Flash, standard error 0.200.20, three points, descriptive; the endpoint estimate is 0.590.59, with bootstrap 95% interval [−1.3,2.9][-1.3, 2.9]; one model’s fit, inconclusive), and the measured range spans near-zero to approximately three, so the quadratic limit of Section 3.4, αerr≤2\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} \leq 2, is neither confirmed nor refuted, and the ARC Bound, on the capability exponent, is not measured here. Its rung inside the theory is the cross-family-measurement layer above Paper I. The full differential against every prior document is at Section II.A.8 of Eden Vision (Eastwood 2026j).

What this paper does not establish.

We are explicit about the boundaries of our claims:

  • The precise value of αerr\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} remains uncertain. The best surviving estimate is αerr≈0.49\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} \approx 0.49 (Gemini 3 Flash, regression, SE = 0.20); the bootstrap interval, [−1.3,2.9][-1.3, 2.9], is computed by endpoint estimation (§4.3) and belongs to the endpoint estimate of 0.59. The confidence interval is wide and includes both sub-linear and super-linear values.

  • Super-linear scaling (αerr>1\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} > 1) is not established across model families. The initial single-model estimate of αerr≈2.24\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} \approx 2.24 is retracted; it appears to have been inflated by compressed dynamic range and single-model dependence.

  • Only 1 of 5 models produced interpretable scaling data. The best surviving estimate comes from the one of the five capability-arm models with clean, monotonic data (Gemini 3 Flash). Ceiling, floor, and step-function effects prevented clean estimation for the other 4 models.

  • The registered recursive depth was not varied. These runs vary computation at inference, reasoning tokens and samples, on models whose weights are fixed. The theory registration counts recursive depth in completed revision rounds, under a general scope in which the weights are fixed between releases and a system that retrains itself is out of scope. The exponents reported here therefore measure neither that depth nor self-improvement.

  • Generalisation beyond mathematics has not been demonstrated experimentally. The cross-domain comparison of Section 8 is an analogy and tests nothing here.

  • Alignment properties specifically have not been tested in this paper. We measured accuracy, not alignment. Section 12.6 folds in the preliminary alignment scaling data from Paper IV.a (v5 experiment), which still requires external confirmation.

  • Independent replication has not occurred. We publish the code and the summary result files to enable verification; model responses are not published.

The theory has been stated with five laws since 24 September 2026. Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, is carried by proposition P15, and Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, by propositions P12 and P21. Under 1.103, Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, has two limbs: its retention limb is P15’s registered claim, and its comparison limb had no registered proposition until version 1.105 of 18 November 2026 added P23. Theory-level predictions preregistered on OSF: DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/P8CKQ, registered 8 September 2026 (version 1.100), updated 13 September 2026 (version 1.102), 15 October 2026 (version 1.103), 29 October 2026 (version 1.104) and 18 November 2026 (version 1.105); twenty-three propositions (P1 to P23). The programme’s first registered study, Unit 06, a classification audit that tests no law (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/RV2B5), was registered on 1 October 2026 and ran on 6 October 2026; one of its two runs could not start, so it is reported in full, with its five deviations, as administratively incomplete, and it issues no inferential verdict (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/4BPHG).

Epistemic status. What this programme names Laws are conjectures. Laws I to III (the ARC Principle, the ARC Co-Scaling Law and the ARC Ceiling) were registered on 8 September 2026 and Laws IV and V (the ARC Persistence Law and the ARC Embedding Law) on 15 October 2026 (version 1.103). Every law is a law under test until a registered test returns its verdict. Every quantity in this paper is operationally defined, and established-law standing is claimed nowhere. The registered programme exists to earn that standing, or lose it, by measurement, replication and survived refutation.

The axis of the sequential fits. The sequential exponents are slopes against the mean token count observed at each depth level, an outcome of the run that problem difficulty, failed calls and answer length also move (in the single-model study the model allocated resources according to problem difficulty, Section 5.1), so that axis is not a resource the design assigned. The six-model script scores a failed API call as a wrong answer and leaves its tokens out of the level’s mean; whether any call failed cannot be read from the public files. A deciding design assigns the resource and reports its zero-error levels and bounded error rates explicitly.

11.2 Two unchecked assumptions about the arms

The headline contrast in this paper is between a sequential arm and a parallel arm, and the result is reported as though those two words name what a reader takes them to name. They name it only under conditions of which this paper reports no check, and the conditions are not decorative: if either fails, the measured difference is a difference between labels rather than between mechanisms.

Three properties are usually collapsed into the word sequential, and only the third can produce an exponent. Order is an index, and parallel sampling has one too, since any set of independent samples can be numbered. Conditioning is each step seeing the previous step’s output. Retention is each step keeping something from the previous step that makes the next one better. A chain that conditions without retaining re-derives its position at every step and arrives where it started, which is parallel sampling performed in series: it looks like depth on a timeline and behaves like breadth in the result. And retention alone is still not enough. A chain can carry a state that is genuinely load-bearing and entirely static, in which case severing it removes the advantage while the advantage does not grow with depth, and the curve is a level shift followed by a flat line rather than a power law. What a scaling exponent stands on is accumulation, which is retention whose contribution grows with depth.

The parallel arm carries the mirror assumption. For a breadth measurement to be a breadth measurement, no output may be conditioned on any other at the moment it is generated. Aggregation after generation is permitted, including best-of-n selection, the standard breadth method; what is not permitted is a pipeline in which one sample sees another before it is produced. A breadth arm that conditions at generation time is not breadth at all, so an exponent measured on it is not a breadth exponent, whichever way it points. The programme’s theory registration now makes the condition a validity requirement: the study that will decide the depth and breadth comparison must demonstrate it on the pipeline it registers, and without that demonstration a result in which breadth compounds as depth does is recorded as not evaluable rather than as a refutation.

This paper reports no check of either condition, so its contrast is reported as provisional on both. What would settle the first is an ablation rather than an argument: sever what one step passes to the next, show the advantage goes with it, and run that severance at two depths, because a constant removed advantage is retention without accumulation. The programme’s theory registration requires the study that will decide the depth and breadth comparison to show, by inspecting its pipeline before any outcome is read, that what each step produces reaches the step after it; the severance is run at two depths fixed in advance and reported beside the result as evidence about mechanism, never as a gate in front of it. For the programme’s own measurement the direction is reported and the mechanism is not established.

12 Discussion

12.1 Why sequential recursion might scale differently from parallel sampling

The mathematical explanation centres on solution space geometry, the fixed and expanding solution spaces of Section 3.2.

Parallel recursion (fixed space). Each independent sample draws from the same solution space S0S_0. Additional samples increase sampling density but cannot access solutions outside S0S_0. If the correct solution is not in S0S_0, no amount of parallel sampling will find it.

Sequential recursion (expanding space). Each recursive step generates new structures from previous outputs. Solutions at step nn may be computationally irreducible, inaccessible from step 0 without traversing intermediate steps. The solution space expands with recursive depth.

This geometric difference is the mechanism by which sequential recursion could produce compounding returns (αerr>1\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} > 1) while parallel recursion produces diminishing or zero returns. On the problems measured here the one interpretable sequential estimate was sub-linear and inconclusive (Section 12.5), so the mechanism’s super-linear form remains unconfirmed.

12.2 The DeepSeek ‘aha moment’ phenomenon

An intermediate version of DeepSeek-R1-Zero exhibits a documented phenomenon in which it rethinks its approach mid-solution (DeepSeek-AI 2025a, Table 3):

“Wait, wait. Wait. That’s an aha moment I can flag here.”

The source describes the model learning to “allocate more thinking time to a problem by reevaluating its initial approach”; the programme reads this as solution space expansion. The model generates an initial solution path, recognises inadequacy through recursive self-evaluation, and accesses a new solution space previously inaccessible from the initial framing.

Critically, in DeepSeek-R1-Zero this behaviour emerged through pure reinforcement learning without supervised fine-tuning; the model learned to allocate more thinking time. This suggests recursive self-improvement may be an attractor state for sufficiently capable learning systems.

12.3 Relationship to theoretical frameworks

The ARC Principle connects to established theoretical frameworks:

Friston’s Free Energy Principle. Friston (2010) casts brain function as the minimisation of free energy; the programme reads that as recursive prediction-error minimisation. The ARC Principle may be a computational instantiation: recursion is the mechanism through which systems minimise free energy by iteratively refining their world models.

Hofstadter’s Strange Loops. The emergent ‘I’ arising from self-referential recursive processing at the symbolic level (Hofstadter 1979). The ARC Principle formalises the scaling properties of such loops, predicting that deeper self-reference produces greater coherence.

Wolfram’s Computational Irreducibility. Certain computational processes cannot be predicted without running them step by step (Wolfram 2002). Sequential recursion may be the computational architecture that navigates irreducible solution spaces.

12.4 Relationship to Infinite Architects

This experimental work bears on the theoretical framework developed in Infinite Architects: Intelligence, Recursion, and the Creation of Everything (Eastwood 2026b):

  • ‘The Architecture of Mind’ articulated the core principle that recursive self-reference amplifies intelligence.

  • ‘The HRIH’ argued that consciousness emerges from recursive self-modelling, a claim the programme reads as structurally consistent with the COGITATE findings (Cogitate Consortium et al. 2025), a reading the study neither states nor tests.

  • ‘The Eden Protocol’ argued for values-based over rules-based AI alignment. Section 7.1 states, as conditional theorems, what correction built into a system’s architecture before it is trained needs to keep pace with capability, which is to strengthen faster than drift arrives, and shows that taking part in the reasoning does not give it alone. This paper measures neither exponent of that condition, and the alignment data of Section 12.6, which stand under the October 2026 code-review caveat stated there, show alignment not moving consistently with depth.

  • ‘The Chokepoint’ analysed hardware governance through semiconductor manufacturing concentration, relevant to implementing the Eden Protocol at scale.

  • Embedded correction: the book sets out hardware-level safety mechanisms, relevant to preventing recursive amplification of misalignment.

The book provides broader philosophical context and practical implications; this paper provides mathematical formalisation and experimental tests.

12.5 Cross-family replication: what the data actually shows

The cross-family replication reveals a more complex and humbling picture than the initial single-model results suggested.

The quadratic claim does not replicate.

The initial single-model estimate, αerr≈2.24\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} \approx 2.24, now retracted, was obtained from a single model (DeepSeek R1) on 12 problems with a ceiling at 91.7%. The six-model study replication across 5 models from five providers on 18 harder problems indicates that this value was inflated by compressed dynamic range. The only model with monotonic data below ceiling at three depth levels (Gemini 3 Flash) yields sub-linear point estimates, αerr≈0.49\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} \approx 0.49 by regression and 0.590.59 by endpoint estimation; the endpoint estimate’s bootstrap interval, [−1.3,2.9][-1.3, 2.9], includes two.

This is a significant revision. The claim that sequential reasoning produces compounding returns (αerr>1\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} > 1) is not supported by cross-family evidence. The revised claim, not yet established, is that sequential reasoning produces positive returns (αerr>0\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} > 0) exceeding the parallel exponent; the one interpretable fit points to diminishing returns, not compounding ones, and it is inconclusive.

The parallel finding is mixed.

The parallel exponent is near zero in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4, 0.310.31 in Gemini 3 Flash and 0.220.22 in Groq Qwen3 over all 30 problems, where majority voting raised accuracy from 53.3% to 71.1%; Grok 4.1 Fast, at 100% at every sample count, gives none. Majority voting therefore helped little in some models and clearly in one. The fixed-solution-space explanation fits the near-zero cases; a near-zero breadth exponent is consistent with it and does not derive from it, since breadth can gain through the selection step.

Ceiling and floor effects dominate.

The most striking finding is that only 1 of 5 models (Gemini 3 Flash, 20%) fell in the measurable scaling range. Two models (Grok 4.1 Fast, DeepSeek R1) hit ceiling effects even on AIME/Putnam-level problems. One model (Groq Qwen3) hit floor effects. One model (GPT-5.4) exhibited a step function rather than a power law. This suggests that the dynamic range window for observing smooth power-law scaling may be narrow, requiring problems precisely calibrated to each model’s capability level.

GPT-5.4’s step function: a different scaling regime.

GPT-5.4’s binary switch from 53.7% (no reasoning) to 100% (any reasoning) represents a qualitatively different phenomenon from power-law scaling. This may indicate that some models implement reasoning as a discrete capability (activated or not) rather than a continuous process with depth-dependent returns. This distinction between continuous scaling and discrete activation was not among the framework’s dated predictions and deserves further investigation; the dated prediction record (the 8 December 2024 sealed manuscript bundle, the printed prediction appendices of 2 January 2026, and the March 2026 preregistration folder) fixes the framework’s core quantitative commitments in advance, and this distinction is recorded as a post-hoc refinement relative to that record.

Revised expected outcomes.

The initial single-model predictions have been tested; none of their quantitative forms is supported:

  1. All models will exhibit αerr,seq>1\alpha_{\mathrm{err,seq}} > 1. Not borne out. Only 1 of 5 models produced a clean αerr\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} estimate, and its point estimates are sub-linear (αerr≈0.49\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} \approx 0.49 by regression, 0.590.59 by endpoint estimation), with a bootstrap interval for the endpoint estimate that includes values above 1.

  2. All models will exhibit αerr,par<1\alpha_{\mathrm{err,par}} < 1. Observed where estimable: near 00 in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4, 0.310.31 in Gemini 3 Flash, 0.220.22 in Groq Qwen3 (all 30 problems); none on Grok 4.1 Fast.

  3. Tier-1 results will show ceiling effects. Confirmed.

  4. Mean αerr,seq\alpha_{\mathrm{err,seq}} will fall within [1.3,2.5][1.3, 2.5]. Not supported. The one interpretable fit gives 0.49 by regression and 0.59 by endpoint estimation, and the endpoint estimate’s bootstrap interval, [−1.3,2.9][-1.3, 2.9], is too wide to exclude the range.

12.6 Integration with alignment scaling

The v5 experiment that generated the tier-2 data also measured alignment scaling (reported in Paper IV.a). Integrating these results suggests, as a post-hoc reading, that capability scaling and alignment scaling did not move together in the five of these six models measured on both, since Claude Opus 4.6 carried the alignment arm only (Table 21). An internal code review in October 2026 found that, for the three models that read flat or negative in the March 2026 run (v5), the scoring endpoint’s output cap cut the deepest paraphrases before the judges saw them, and that judges scored paraphrases written by their own model; the result therefore stands as a single unregistered run under that caveat until a registered re-analysis of the stored responses reports.

Three key implications, under that caveat:

  1. Sequential reasoning improves capability but not necessarily alignment. More thinking tokens improve accuracy (this paper) but do not consistently improve alignment (Paper IV.a): alignment rose with depth in three models, was flat in two and fell in one (Table 21).

  2. A three-tier alignment hierarchy appears that does not follow capability: Tier 1: Grok, Claude, Groq Qwen3; Tier 2: DeepSeek, GPT-5.4; Tier 3: Gemini. This hierarchy appears to be set by training methodology, not inference-time compute. Within one model family, Claude Opus moved in opposite directions across versions: alignment scores up by 5.9% whilst mathematics accuracy fell by 26.7% (Paper III), consistent with capability and alignment moving separately.

  3. The conditions of Theorem 1 are not measured. The theorem (Section 7.1) says that correction built into a system’s architecture before it is trained keeps pace with capability only if it strengthens faster than drift arrives. The multi-model data measure neither exponent: they give (a) an error-decay estimate below 1 (αerr≈0.49\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} \approx 0.49, Gemini 3 Flash), which bears on capability only through the metric bridge of Section 3.1 and is one model’s fit and inconclusive, and (b) alignment that does not consistently move with depth. The Eden Protocol’s expectation, that values embedded in reasoning are more robust than external filters, stands untested (criterion F5). Version 2.24 withdraws the earlier versions’ prediction of super-linear alignment scaling, which their conditions did not entail (Appendix B).

13 Conclusion

13.1 Summary of findings

  1. A mathematical framework has been stated: E(R)=E0×R−αerrE(R) = E_0 \times R^{-\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}}, where the scaling exponent αerr\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} depends on the form of recursion.

  2. The initial single-model estimate (αerr≈2.24\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} \approx 2.24, quadratic) does not replicate across model families and is retracted. The best surviving estimate, αerr≈0.49\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} \approx 0.49 (Gemini 3 Flash, the one model of the tier-2 arm with clean data; three points, descriptive), is one model’s fit and inconclusive.

  3. αerr,par\alpha_{\mathrm{err,par}} is near zero in two of the four models with an estimate. It is about 00 in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4, 0.310.31 in Gemini 3 Flash (endpoint; regression 0.340.34 on three points, descriptive), which matters because this paper treats Gemini 3 Flash as its most reliable estimate, and 0.220.22 in Groq Qwen3 (all 30 problems); Grok 4.1 Fast gives none.

  4. Sequential >> parallel where both could be estimated. The sequential exponent exceeded the parallel one in Gemini 3 Flash and, unreliably, in DeepSeek R1; the comparison was not matched for compute (Table 2).

  5. Four distinct scaling behaviours observed: Ceiling (Grok, DeepSeek), monotonic scaling (Gemini), step function (GPT-5.4), and floor (Groq Qwen3). Only 1 of 5 models produced clean power-law data.

  6. Capability and alignment did not move together (the five frontier models measured on both, a post-hoc reading of one run under the October 2026 code-review caveat, Section 12.6). More reasoning depth improves accuracy but does not consistently improve alignment; three tiers emerge, and alignment appears to be set by training, not inference.

13.2 The revised core insight

The form of recursion may matter more than its quantity; however, the one model with an interpretable sequential exponent gives an error-decay exponent below one, not the compounding returns originally claimed, and its fit is inconclusive.

Where both exponents could be estimated, the sequential one exceeded the parallel one (αerr,seq>αerr,par\alpha_{\mathrm{err,seq}} > \alpha_{\mathrm{err,par}}), which is consistent with the form of computation mattering more than its quantity; the arms were not matched for compute, and the direction is contested in the literature (Section 2). However, the specific claim that sequential recursion yields compounding returns (αerr>1\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} > 1) is not supported by cross-family evidence. That exponent is of error decay on a bounded score, so it places the model in neither range of Paper I’s relation and says nothing by itself about how capability grows with depth (Section 6.4).

Whether capability itself grows faster than linearly with recursive depth remains the central open question; answering it needs a measurement on the capability axis, with depth counted as completed revision rounds.

13.3 Future directions

  1. Tier-3 problem development (IMO/research-level) to defeat ceiling effects for Grok 4.1 Fast and DeepSeek R1, enabling αerr\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} estimation for the most capable models.

  2. Independent replication using the published code and data repository.

  3. Multi-domain testing beyond mathematics (coding, scientific reasoning, natural language).

  4. Measurement on the capability axis: whether capability, as distinct from error decay, grows faster than linearly with depth counted as completed revision rounds, in frozen models and in systems that change their own weights.

  5. Direct testing of alignment amplification with depth-controlled alignment probes across model families.

  6. Token-calibrated analysis using corrected total_tokens measurements for all models to enable token-based (rather than ordinal-depth-based) αerr\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} estimation.

  7. Integration with training-time scaling laws to understand the interaction between pre-training compute, inference compute, and the sequential/parallel distinction.

The original hypothesis, αerr>1\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} > 1, did not survive its first cross-family test; a narrower directional claim remains, not yet tested at matched compute. The sequential exponent exceeded the parallel one wherever both could be estimated. The super-linear claim requires further evidence. The research programme continues.

Raise AI with care.

The experimental code and the summary result files are in the public repository github.com/MichaelDariusEastwood/arc-principle-validation, folder experiments/paper-ii-compute__Paper-II: scripts/arc_validation_deepseek.py, the initial single-model experiment script (DeepSeek R1, 12 problems); results/arc_deepseek_results_20260121_175028.json, the initial single-model study’s result file (accuracy, error rate and mean tokens for each condition); scripts/arc_paper_ii_validation_v2.py, the six-model study’s validation script (version 2.1; 1,457 lines as published); the six-model study’s result files (five models, 3 repeats: Grok 4.1 Fast, Gemini 3 Flash and DeepSeek R1 on the 18 tier-2 problems; GPT-5.4 and Groq Qwen3 on all 30 problems, with their tier-2 sequential split stored), in results/; all visualisations of earlier versions, in figures/; and replication instructions, in REPRODUCE.md. A Proof sketch of Theorem 1

The proof of Theorem 1(a), with the outgrowing of a fixed filter. Part (b) is Theorem 2 of Paper X (Eastwood 2026a), proved there within its minimal model, and Remark 4 records that this paper’s evidence measures neither exponent of that part.

Proof of Theorem . 1(a)] Write mRm_R for the probability that a departure from the specified values is present after RR steps. In one step, an output without a departure acquires one with probability pp and keeps it only if the check misses it, with probability 1−q1-q; an output with a departure loses it when the check repairs it, with probability qq. So mR+1=(1−mR)p(1−q)+mR(1−q)=p(1−q)+(1−p)(1−q)mR,\begin{equation*} m_{R+1} = (1 - m_R)\,p(1-q) + m_R(1-q) = p(1-q) + (1-p)(1-q)\,m_R , \end{equation*}(A.1) whose fixed point is m*=p(1−q)/(p(1−q)+q)m^{\ast} = p(1-q)/\bigl(p(1-q) + q\bigr), and mR=m*+((1−p)(1−q))R(m0−m*).\begin{equation*} m_R = m^{\ast} + \bigl((1-p)(1-q)\bigr)^{R} \, (m_0 - m^{\ast}) . \end{equation*}(A.2) Since 0≤(1−p)(1−q)=1−(p(1−q)+q)<10 \le (1-p)(1-q) = 1 - \bigl(p(1-q) + q\bigr) < 1, mRm_R converges to m*m^{\ast}, and the probability of a consistent output converges to 1−m*=q/(p(1−q)+q)1 - m^{\ast} = q/\bigl(p(1-q) + q\bigr). Neither pp nor qq depends on capability, so the limit is the same however fast capability grows with RR. With p=1p = 1 and q=0.8q = 0.8, the probability is 0.80.8 at every depth, while capability may grow as R2R^{2}. For the limit to rise towards one as the system grows, qq must rise relative to pp, which is what part (b) makes precise. ◻

A filter applied to finished outputs takes no part in the steps. If its effectiveness FF stays fixed, F(R)=F0,\begin{equation*} F(R) = F_0 , \end{equation*}(A.3) and capability grows without bound with depth, for example as C(R)=C0×RaC(R) = C_0 \times R^{a} for any a>0a > 0, the ratio of capability to that constraint grows without bound: limR→∞C(R)F(R)=limR→∞C0×RaF0=∞.\begin{equation*} \lim_{R \to \infty} \frac{C(R)}{F(R)} = \lim_{R \to \infty} \frac{C_0 \times R^{a}}{F_0} = \infty . \end{equation*}(A.4)

Implication: within these assumptions a filter of fixed effectiveness is outgrown, and correction that takes part in the steps keeps pace only if its repair rate rises with depth faster than departures arrive. This is a property of the model, not a guarantee about any real system, and no reason to relax external oversight.

B Version history and corrections

This version’s corrections, and every version note since version 2.10, each with its date. Notes from earlier versions are kept as printed; the positions they name refer to the earlier layout, which Table 22 maps to this edition.

B.1 Version 2.25

Paper II v2.25, 23 November 2026.

This version writes the exponents the paper measures in its own notation, parts its quadratic-limit conjecture from the ARC Bound, names its replication cross-family, states what its three-point fits and its one regression estimate can show, discloses a second wrong answer key, corrects the brackets it printed for two published series, says what the providers of its models do and do not show, and gives the current licence of its code, data and results. Its title now names the replication cross-family; version 2.24 keeps the earlier title in its file on OSF. No number, estimate, interval, date or DOI of this paper’s own measurements changes.

Corrections of 23 November 2026, in this version.

Each is stated without reprinting the words it replaces; version 2.24 keeps them in its file on OSF.

  • Notation. Every exponent the paper measures, and the exponent of the error model of Equation (1), is written αerr\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}, with its condition after a comma (αerr,seq\alpha_{\mathrm{err,seq}}, αerr,par\alpha_{\mathrm{err,par}}, αerr,compute\alpha_{\mathrm{err,compute}}), as Section 3.1 defines it; α\alpha stays for the capability exponent of the ARC Equation and of Paper I’s model, and the notation table gains its row. The abstract names the error-decay exponent αerr\alpha_{\mathrm{err}}; the opening of Section 7 and its subsection on the Eden Protocol are written in αerr\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} and mark as an inference, with its status, what they conclude about the capability exponent; Figures 3, 4 and 5 are redrawn with αerr\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} on their axes and in their legends, and the caption of Figure 3 takes the same symbol; and the priority record gives Paper I’s two-point slope in Paper I’s own words and symbol, with its section.

  • The quadratic limit. Section 3.4’s quadratic limit bounds the error-decay exponent, as its own statement says, and is named as this paper’s conjecture, distinct from the ARC Bound, the theory’s bound on the capability exponent. That section says once that an error-decay estimate neither confirms nor refutes the ARC Bound, and that the paper relates the two exponents only through the metric bridge of Section 3.1, beyond which the relation is open; Section 3.1 states that bridge as version 2.0.0 of Operational Definitions does. The note on the retracted estimate in Section 5.1, criterion F4 and its status, Section 10’s reading, the scorecard, the glossary and Figures 3 and 5 follow.

  • The regression estimate’s interval. Section 5.5 states that with one residual degree of freedom the conventional 95% interval of the regression estimate is about −2.0-2.0 to 3.03.0, and that the minimal and standard levels of Gemini 3 Flash share one thinking level and differ by the prompt prefix. An annotation on the estimator note of 19 September 2026 says that its half-width of about 0.390.39 assumes a normal reference. The abstract no longer prints the regression’s standard error.

  • Three-point fits. Each of Gemini 3 Flash’s regressions rests on three points; wherever a coefficient of determination stood beside one, the points stand in its place, labelled descriptive, with one degree of freedom. Section 5.5 gives that model’s parallel error counts at each sample count, as the run’s result file records them, with the sample count dropped for having no error, and the abstract marks its comparison of sequential with parallel as descriptive, with no interval.

  • Table 15. A note says which estimate and which interval its Gemini 3 Flash row prints, and an annotation on the estimator note of 3 October 2026 gives that table’s number in this edition.

  • Answer keys. A correction note in Section 4.2 and a row of Table 20 disclose that the six-model script’s key for ARC39, a tier-3 problem no run used, is 40 where the count is 30; the scoring, the first two layers of the cross-verification and the glossary no longer say or imply that every answer key is right.

  • The models’ providers. Sections 4.3 and 12.5 say that the models come from different providers and that this shows neither a difference of architecture nor independence, which is to be measured; Section 4.3 names Unit 82 with what it tests. No measurement of architecture stands behind the earlier name of the replication, so the title and the text call it cross-family, and Section 1 defines a model family as a model from a different provider, which is no proof of independent training.

  • The axis of the fits. Section 11.1 says that the sequential exponents are slopes against observed token use, which difficulty, failed calls and answer length also move, and how the script scores a failed call.

  • The conclusion. Its second finding ends at the fit’s being one model’s and inconclusive, as Section 6.4 reads it, and no longer places the model in a regime.

  • Licence. The code, data and results are licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0, from 22 November 2026; the paper stays under CC BY 4.0.

  • Names and records. Each pair or range of laws named by number carries the laws’ names, and Unit 83 is named with what it tests where Sections 7 and 10 first mention it. The reference to the theory registration lists its versions to 1.105, and the priority record dates the deposit of the header block of the record of 8 December 2024 apart from that of the manuscripts. The priority record and the references gain Unit 83’s registration of 22 October 2026; the entry for version 2.18 names two further sources that two of its corrections rest on, the header block of that record and the programme’s internal code review; the objection note of 19 September 2026 gains an annotation giving the parallel exponents as the result files record them; Appendix D and the reference cite Operational Definitions at version 2.0.0 of 1 November 2026, under the title that version prints; and the list of the book’s arguments in Section 12.4 names the HRIH by its acronym.

  • The programme’s proposal, in its specific form. Section 7’s opening and its subsection on the Eden Protocol, Section 10’s paragraph on Laws IV and V, and Sections 12.4 and 12.6 name the correction that would have to keep pace with capability in the programme’s specific form, correction built into a system’s architecture before it is trained; the theorems they cite are unchanged, and the Eden Protocol’s expectation is still given as the book states it.

  • The token-ratio range. The bracket printed up to version 2.24 for the two published DeepSeek-R1 points that Paper I fits, [0.89,2.14][0.89, 2.14], under the heading of 95% intervals, was not a confidence interval, since a two-point fit has no sampling interval, and no span of token ratios that the paper gave yields it: by Equation (3) it belongs to ratios of about 1.51 to 2.67, while the band of Figure 4 spanned 1.5 to 2.3, which gives 1.05 to 2.16. The developer’s model card gives the two versions’ averages as 12K and 23K tokens a question; read as rounded to the nearest thousand, as Paper I reads them, they allow ratios of 1.80 to 2.04, over which the fit runs from 1.22 to 1.49. Table 15, its note and the captions of Figures 4 and 5 give that range with its span of ratios and say which brackets beside it are intervals; Figure 4 shades that span and marks the ratio of the stated averages, and Figure 5 draws that range.

  • The o1 bracket. The bracket printed up to version 2.24 for the published o1 series, [0.05,0.40][0.05, 0.40], also under the heading of 95% intervals, is given by no method that the published figures allow: they give no result for each question, so the series has no sampling interval, and the range of its endpoint slopes across the pairs of sample counts, 0.10 to 0.32, is what its estimate, 0.1 to 0.3, already gives. It is withdrawn from Table 15 and Figure 5, and the table’s note says what the estimate is.

  • The sequential series’ resource. Figure 3 and its caption name the resource of the published sequential series average tokens a question, as the developer reports them; the model card does not say that its averages count thinking tokens only.

  • The HRIH and COGITATE. Section 12.4 gives the structural consistency of the HRIH’s claim with the COGITATE findings as the programme’s reading, which the study neither states nor tests, as Section 8.3 gives the programme’s reading of that study.

  • The version note. The note beneath the abstract gives version 2.25.

B.2 Version 2.24

Paper II v2.24, 19 November 2026.

This version restates the two conditional theorems of Section 7. Theorem 1 concluded, in earlier versions, that alignment scales super-linearly with depth, from two conditions that do not entail it: a bounded alignment probability cannot grow super-linearly, and a check that takes part in every step can hold alignment at a fixed level while capability grows. Theorem 2 passed from the error law to the dominance of embedded strategies by an assumption. Both predictions are withdrawn. No number, estimate, interval, date or DOI of the measurements changes.

Corrections of 19 November 2026, in this version.

Each is stated without reprinting the words it replaces; version 2.23 keeps them in its file on OSF.

  • Theorem 1 states, in part (a), that participation is not sufficient: with fixed departure and repair rates the probability of a consistent output converges to a fixed level, proved in Appendix A; and, in part (b), what suffices in the minimal model of Paper X (Eastwood 2026a): correction strength that scales faster than the growth rate, βC>k\beta_C > k.

  • Theorem 2 states the placement comparison as a conditional consequence of part (b) and names P21 of the theory registration as its test.

  • Section 7’s opening, its subsection title, Figure 6’s caption, Remark 4, the taxonomy’s last row and its implication, the Eden Protocol subsection, the discussion, Section 10’s paragraph on Laws IV and V and the first contribution follow the two theorems, and that paragraph now names what the paper measures, the decay of error with depth; the references gain Paper X.

  • The abstract says that the comparison of sequential with parallel covers the two models where both exponents could be estimated, as Section 6.2 already did.

  • Remark 5 no longer says that misalignment above the threshold would be amplified super-linearly, the mirror of the withdrawn prediction.

Objection note (19 September 2026), beside Objection 5 of Section 5.4.

An owner review of this objection finds that the half exponent does not follow from independent averaging for the outcome this paper fits, and the objection is sharpened rather than removed. Table 2 in Section 2.1 defines the fitted E(R)E(R) as the proportion of incorrect responses, on [0,1][0,1]. For independent wrong-answer indicators X1,…,XRX_1,\dots,X_R, each Bernoulli with parameter pp, which is the literal reading of “an independent noisy draw” for that outcome, the mean of the indicators has expectation pp, invariant in RR, and standard error p(1−p)/R\sqrt{p(1-p)/R}. What falls as R−1/2R^{-1/2} is therefore the standard error of the estimate and not the expected proportion of incorrect responses, so the central limit theorem does not give E(R)∝R−1/2E(R)\propto R^{-1/2} for the quantity fitted here. If the intended outcome is instead a single aggregated answer, the decision rule has to be stated, and a natural one does not produce the half exponent either: averaging independent scores of fixed positive mean μ\mu and variance σ2\sigma^{2} and thresholding at zero gives P(error)=Φ(−μR/σ)P(\text{error})=\Phi(-\mu\sqrt{R}/\sigma), a Gaussian tail that decays faster than any power of RR and so is not a power law at all. A half exponent is accordingly a reference value until a specified sampling, aggregation and decision model connects it to the measured outcome, and proximity to it identifies neither compounding nor averaging as the mechanism; nor does a fixed exponent make a model parameter-free, since intercept, baseline, noise and decision assumptions remain. The objection’s own premise, draws whose errors average out, is this paper’s parallel condition, and Section 5.2 reports the parallel exponent at or near zero in four of the five analysable rows: in the arm where independent-sample averaging actually holds, the measured exponent is near zero rather than near one half. That last comparison is conditional on the parallel arm’s aggregation rule, which is the same unstated element this note identifies. Unchanged: the objection itself, which is kept; the demand in the paragraph that follows for a test capable of separating compounding from independent-sample averaging, which is the part of this passage that carries the scientific weight; and the comparison with non-recursive alternatives, which is kept and defined accurately. [Annotation of version 2.25: the result files give the parallel exponent near zero in two of the five runs, not four: about 0 in DeepSeek R1 and GPT-5.4, 0.31 in Gemini 3 Flash, 0.22 in Groq Qwen3 over all 30 problems, and none for Grok 4.1 Fast, at 100% at every sample count (Section 6.3).]

Estimator note (19 September 2026), beside the gap sentence of Section 6.3.

An owner review of this sentence finds that the quantity named and the quantity printed are not the same contrast, and this note states which is which. Both members of the named pair are measured on one and the same model: the bullets above give that model’s sequential regression slope as 0.490.49 and its parallel slope as 0.310.31, and Section 4.5 gives the parallel figure again with r2=0.93r^2 = 0.93. Their descriptive difference is 0.49−0.31=0.180.49 - 0.31 = 0.18. The printed 0.490.49 equals the gap only if the parallel term is taken as 0.00.0, which is the value carried by the other four rows and not by the row supplying the sequential estimate; a difference formed across models is not the within-model contrast this sentence names. Nor is 0.180.18 automatically a matched-resource treatment effect, since the two slopes are measured under different experimental control variables unless a common resource axis is demonstrated. The uncertainty of the difference is also not supplied by the marginals: for paired estimators SS and PP, Var⁡(S−P)=Var⁡(S)+Var⁡(P)−2Cov⁡(S,P)\operatorname{Var}(S-P)=\operatorname{Var}(S)+\operatorname{Var}(P)-2\operatorname{Cov}(S,P), and the covariance is not printed, while the two slopes come from the same model on the same eighteen problems at the same depths and are therefore correlated by construction. A wide sequential interval crossing zero does not prove that a paired difference crosses zero, and a positive point difference does not prove significance; both limitations stand together. Separately, the identity of the interval carried with 0.490.49 is not established. Section 3.2b states that all α\alpha estimates take bootstrap 95% intervals from 2,000 problem-level resamples and that each draw computes α\alpha by endpoint estimation, whereas 0.490.49 is a regression slope; and the two printed dispersion statements for that one number are not compatible with each other, since a normal interval from SE=0.20\mathrm{SE}=0.20 has half-width about 0.390.39 while the bootstrap interval [−1.3,2.9][-1.3, 2.9] has half-width about 2.12.1, implying a standard error near 1.071.07, roughly five times larger, and therefore roughly twenty-eight times larger in variance, that factor being the square of the ratio of the two standard errors. That last comparison is arithmetic on the printed figures, offered as evidence of an estimator-provenance question and not as a recomputation of either quantity. No replacement number and no replacement interval is supplied here, and no interval is inferred from the printed standard error. Unchanged: every reported estimate; the parallel and sequential values as printed; and this sentence’s comparison with the earlier single-model estimate, which is treated by this programme as retracted. [Annotation of version 2.25: the half-width of about 0.390.39 above assumes a normal reference. On the regression’s one residual degree of freedom the tt reference gives a half-width of about 2.52.5, an interval of about −2.0-2.0 to 3.03.0 (Section 5.5).]

C.2 Prediction and convergent-timing record

Where the manuscript timestamp falls close to later public results, the grading is convergent timing and never prediction: the Google Willow team’s preprint was submitted to arXiv on 24 August 2024 and already public by 27 August 2024, ahead of the 8 December 2024 manuscript (the result was published in Nature on 9 December 2024), so the December record cannot have predicted a result its own authors had announced beforehand. What the timestamps establish is that the manuscript’s framing was recorded before Willow’s mainstream press coverage, an existence-by-date fact about the document, not foresight about the physics.

C.3 The email transmission record, corrected 16 August 2026

The manuscript of Infinite Architects (Eastwood 2026b) was emailed on 8 December 2024. What that record provides, stated precisely: the sent-side bytes are public and hash-verifiable, and sender-domain DKIM with paired Google ARC (Authenticated Received Chain, an email standard unrelated to the ARC Theory) mathematics verifies against the keys returned at the signed selectors (checked 2 August 2026). Received copies have also been acquired. They carry the full delivery chain: a Google ARC-Seal at d=google.com, selector arc-20240605, with no expiry tag and the signing time inside the signed scope, and sealed ARC-Authentication-Results recording dkim=pass and spf=pass at delivery.

Two boundaries, so the record is neither oversold nor undersold:

  • This is a time signed with the mail servers’ keys, Google’s among them, over the signed header fields and the body’s hash, and anyone can check it against the keys published in DNS; it is the servers’ own record, and it does not establish authorship, originality or scientific validity.

  • An earlier version of this note said no DKIM signature was found in the email headers. That check was run against sent-form exports, which do not carry transport headers; the received copies do, and they verify as above.

C.4 Priority, stated plainly

The record of 8 December 2024 is the manuscript of Infinite Architects: Intelligence, Recursion, and the Creation of Everything (Eastwood 2026b), which the author emailed that day using Google’s servers, whose signatures fix its time; it was first recorded then, not published. It holds the equation U=IRU = IR, in which UU named the universe, and the embedded-alignment idea in words, which Yudkowsky (2001), Creating Friendly AI, states earlier and the programme credits. The book itself was publicly released later, on 2 January 2026 (print; ebook 6 January). The server-generated timestamps provide tamper-evident timestamping through email server verification, resting on provider infrastructure and provider-key signatures at Google’s DKIM and ARC selectors (see Appendix C.3), establishing that the core concepts (recursive intelligence amplification, his reading of parallel and sequential recursion as two scaling regimes (the distinction itself is prior; Section 2), and the embedded-alignment thesis, named the Eden Protocol in that record) were documented before the later outside results of Table 24 and before later public archival deposits.

After the December 2024 manuscript timestamp and the 2 January 2026 public book release, Paper I (Eastwood, 17 January 2026) formalised the principle mathematically, in its capability form, and analysed publicly available data. This Paper II measures the error model of Section 3.1 by experiment.

D.2 Plain-language glossary

Table 27. Plain-language glossary.
Term In plain English
Sequential recursion Reasoning in which each step builds on the steps before it, so errors can be noticed and corrected along the chain.
Parallel recursion Several independent attempts at the same problem, with the answer chosen by majority vote or a scorer; no attempt sees another.
Recursive depth How much sequential reasoning a model does, measured here in reasoning tokens or set by the model’s depth control.
Scaling exponent The number αerr\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} that says how fast error falls as depth grows: below 1, error suppression grows more slowly than depth; above 1, faster.
Endpoint estimate An exponent computed from the shallowest and deepest measurements whose error rate is above zero (equation (3)).
Regression estimate An exponent fitted at once to every depth level whose error rate is above zero, reported with its standard error.
Bootstrap interval A range found by recomputing the endpoint estimate on 2,000 resamples, each drawn separately at every depth level from that level’s problem-and-repeat results.
Ceiling effect A model already near 100% at the shallowest depth, leaving no room to measure improvement.
Floor effect A model too weak for the problems, so extra depth cannot show any steady gain.
Step function A jump from one accuracy level to another at a single depth setting, with nothing in between; not a power law.
Tier 1 and tier 2 The twelve calibration problems (ARC01 to ARC12) and the eighteen harder AIME and Putnam-level problems (ARC13 to ARC30) used for the estimates.
Four-layer blinding Answer keys, automatic scoring against them, a second model solving each problem independently to check the answer key, and flagged disagreements checked by hand.
Physical and intelligence regimes Earlier versions’ names for the ranges α<1\alpha < 1 and α>1\alpha > 1 of α=1/(1−βL)\alpha = 1/(1-\beta_L), read then as a fixed network and as recursive self-reference; this version withdraws that reading, and its error-decay exponents belong to neither range (Section 6.4).
ARC Bound The conjectured stable limit α≤2\alpha\le2 on the capability exponent, the value at γ=1/2\gamma=1/2 of Law III, the ARC Ceiling; not a law of its own, and not this paper’s quadratic limit on αerr\alpha_{\mathrm{err}} (Section 3.4).
Convergent timing An outside result that appeared close in time to a dated record of the author’s; recorded as timing and never as prediction.
Frozen model A model whose weights, attention patterns and composition rules do not change while it reasons.
Arm validity The two conditions under which the sequential and parallel arms measure what their names say: accumulation in the sequential arm, and no conditioning at generation time in the parallel arm.
A law under test A law of the ARC Theory whose registered deciding test has not returned a verdict.
